p1-v1.alt: The Phoenix lander drifts down under a striped parachute over the icy plains of northern Mars.

textos.texto: May 2008. The Phoenix lander arrives in the Martian Arctic to study its frozen ground.
Hello, Mars! It's so cold here!

p1-v2.alt: Phoenix on the ground with its two round solar panels open and its robotic arm ready.

textos.texto: Phoenix opened its two round solar panels and got its robotic arm ready to dig.
Ready to work!

p1-v3.alt: Phoenix's arm digs a trench in the ground and uncovers bright white chunks.

textos.texto: Its arm dug a shallow trench and found something white and shiny under the dust.
What's that white stuff?

p1-v4.alt: Two photos of the same trench: the first shows small white chunks and in the second they are almost gone. Earth smiles.

textos.texto: Days later, several white chunks were gone: they had turned into vapor. It was water ice!
Confirmed! There's water ice under the Martian ground.
First day
Days later

p2-v1.alt: The InSight lander parachutes down toward a smooth, reddish plain on Mars.

textos.texto: November 2018. Ten years later another lander arrives: InSight. Its mission is to study the inside of Mars.
Hello, Mars! I came to listen to your insides.

p2-v2.alt: With its robotic arm, InSight places a white dome on the ground; a cable connects it to the lander.

textos.texto: With its arm, InSight set a seismometer on the ground and covered it with a protective dome.
Shhh… I'm listening!

p2-v3.alt: Waves from a quake travel up from underground to InSight, which shakes on the surface.

textos.texto: InSight recorded more than 1,300 quakes on Mars. They're called marsquakes!
Mars is shaking! I can feel it!

p2-v4.alt: A cutaway of Mars shows its layers: a thin crust, a thick mantle and a large core at the center.

textos.texto: Waves from the marsquakes showed what Mars is like inside: a crust, a mantle and a large liquid core.
Crust
Mantle

p3-v1.alt: A tired-looking Phoenix covered in frost under a gray winter sky while snow falls.

textos.texto: Phoenix worked for about five months. Then winter came: there was less and less sunlight, and in November 2008 it stopped communicating.

p3-v2.alt: A tired-looking InSight with its solar panels covered in reddish dust.

textos.texto: Dust slowly covered InSight's solar panels. After 4 years of work, it sent its last message in December 2022.
I have very little energy left…

p3-v3.alt: Phoenix on the icy ground next to chunks of ice, and InSight on the red ground next to some waves.

textos.texto: I found water ice under the ground.
And I heard how Mars shakes inside!

p3-v4.alt: A smiling Earth waves at Mars, where tiny Phoenix and InSight can be seen.

textos.texto: Phoenix and InSight taught us that Mars hides secrets beneath its surface: water ice and an interior that still shakes.
Thank you, explorers!

cierre.datoReal: InSight detected more than 1,300 marsquakes. The strongest one, in May 2022, had a magnitude of 4.7.
